rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer:
You pick the order, not timestamps — and the best order gives **6** counters.

**Hardened Scales** and **Doubling Season** are both replacement effects modifying the same event (**Walking Ballista** entering with X = 2 +1/+1 counters, since "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" is a replacement effect per `614.1c`). Per `616.1`, the affected object's controller chooses one to apply; `616.1e` lets either be chosen, and `616.1f` repeats the process with what's left. Timestamps don't matter.

• Hardened Scales first: 2 → "that many plus one" = 3, then doubled → **6**.
• Doubling Season first: 2 → 4, then +1 → **5**.

Each still sees the other's output: per `614.16`, effects that apply "if an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent" also apply when another replacement effect is what's putting them on.

So apply Hardened Scales first and Ballista enters with 6 counters.
citations: rule 616.1: "the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below"
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."

rule 616.1f: "Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply."

rule 614.16: "These replacement effects apply if the effect of a resolving spell or ability creates a token or puts a counter on a permanent, and they also apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so"
rule 614.1c: "Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,”"
oracle 4b515bb0-f275-4400-8032-3173b799ab40#0: "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it."

ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/636b245ed2960105: "If two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a creature you control, you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."

rows.question: opp cast [[Blood Moon]] while i have all three tron lands out. do i still get my 7 mana from urza's? can i tap tower for 3 colorless or is it just a Mountain now
rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer:
No Tron. All three of your lands are just Mountains that tap for {R} — three red mana total, not seven.

**Blood Moon** says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," a type-changing effect in layer 4 (`613.1d`) that sets their land subtype. Per `305.7`, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type." So **Urza's Tower**'s "{T}: Add {C}. If you control an Urza's Mine and an Urza's Power-Plant, add {C}{C}{C} instead" is gone entirely — it has only "{T}: Add {R}".

Even if one of them somehow kept its ability, it wouldn't help: the ability checks land types, not names, and the Urza's Mine/Power-Plant/Tower subtypes have been replaced by Mountain (`205.1a`). They're still nonbasic (`305.8`), so Blood Moon keeps applying to them.
citations: rule 305.7: "It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type."
rule 613.1d: "Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied. These include effects that change an object’s card type, subtype, and/or supertype."
rule 205.1a: "when an effect sets one or more of an object’s subtypes, the new subtype(s) replaces any existing subtypes from the appropriate set"
oracle 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae#0: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."
oracle 32fbb638-ab14-4e8b-a07a-d4c44e3496f2#0: "{T}: Add {C}. If you control an Urza's Mine and an Urza's Power-Plant, add {C}{C}{C} instead."
ruling 32fbb638-ab14-4e8b-a07a-d4c44e3496f2/67514ffa8ee40389: "The ability checks for land types, not the names of other permanents you control."
rule 305.8: "Any land that doesn’t have this supertype is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type."

rows.question: follow up: what if I play [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]] AFTER the moon is already down? urborg has the later timestamp so shouldn't it make everything a Swamp too? my friend says no
rows.expected_answer: Your friend is right. Both effects are layer 4 type-changing effects (613.1d). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's (613.8a): applying Blood Moon makes Urborg a Mountain and strips its rules-text ability (305.7), which removes the existence of Urborg's effect. When a dependency exists it overrides timestamps (613.8), so Blood Moon applies first no matter which entered later (613.8b). Urborg is just a Mountain with '{T}: Add {R}' and nothing becomes a Swamp. (Any actual basic Swamps you control are still Swamps because Blood Moon only affects nonbasic lands.)

outcome.answer:
Your friend is right: playing **Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth** after **Blood Moon** changes nothing — still no Swamps. Urborg is itself a nonbasic land, so Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" sets its subtype to a basic land type, and per `305.7` it "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type." So Urborg's "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types" ability doesn't exist at all, and never generates an effect.

A later timestamp only matters between two effects that both exist in the same layer. Here dependency settles it anyway: Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's, because "applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect" (`613.8a`), and a dependent effect "waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied" (`613.8b`) — Blood Moon applies first regardless of timestamps. Scryfall says the same for the Magus version: it "won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."

Urborg does keep its legendary supertype and is still nonbasic (`305.8`, "Any land that doesn't have this supertype is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type") — it's just a legendary Mountain that taps for {R}.

rows.question: my goyf has two +1/+1 counters on it and I just giant growthed it. opponent [[Clone]]s it. is their clone a huge goyf too or just a regular one? and does the clone even know how big a goyf should be since the p/t is */*+1
rows.expected_answer: Just a regular Tarmogoyf. A copy acquires only the copiable values of the original (707.2): name, mana cost, types, rules text, printed P/T, etc. Counters, Giant Growth's +3/+3, and other non-copy effects are not copiable values, so the Clone gets none of them. The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, and therefore its characteristic-defining ability (707.2a), so the Clone's own P/T is */*+1 computed from card types in graveyards (applied in layer 7a, 613.4a). The copy effect itself is applied in layer 1a (613.2a); your goyf's counters and pump are layer 7c (613.4c) and stay on your goyf only.

outcome.answer:
Their Clone is just a regular **Tarmogoyf** — same size as any Goyf, not pumped and not countered up.

Clone copies only copiable values: "The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object... Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied" (`707.2`). Your +1/+1 counters and the **Giant Growth** effect are not copiable, so neither carries over. Scryfall says the same: Clone "doesn't copy whether that creature is tapped or untapped, whether it has any counters on it or Auras and Equipment attached to it, or any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness, types, color, or so on."

As for the */*+1: the Clone does copy the rules text, which includes the characteristic-defining ability "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1." A copy acquires the abilities of what it copies because they're derived from its rules text (`707.2a`), so the Clone applies that CDA itself and is continuously sized by the graveyards — it doesn't lock in your Goyf's current power/toughness. So if there are 3 card types in graveyards, yours is a 6/7 (3/4 plus two counters plus +3/+3) and theirs is a 3/4.

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every ordinary creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment. Any other non-Aura enchantment Opalescence animates follows Humility itself: its base power and toughness are its mana value when Opalescence is later, and 1/1 when Humility is.

outcome.answer:
With **Humility** already out and **Opalescence** arriving later, Opalescence wins layer 7b.

Layer 4: Opalescence's "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types" animates Humility (and your other non-Aura enchantments); Opalescence does *not* animate itself, so it stays a noncreature enchantment with no P/T and keeps its abilities.

Layer 6: Humility's "All creatures lose all abilities" strips abilities from every creature, including now-creature Humility — but its own continuous effect keeps applying anyway, per `613.6` ("even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process").

Layer 7b: both setting effects live here, so timestamp order decides (`613.4b`, `613.7`). Humility is older, so 1/1 applies first and Opalescence's "base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value" overwrites it. Humility ends up a 4/4 ability-less enchantment creature, and any other non-Aura enchantment is a creature with P/T equal to its mana value. Your ordinary creatures are untouched by Opalescence, so they're still 1/1 with no abilities.

If Opalescence was on the battlefield first, the layers are identical but 7b flips: Opalescence sets mana-value P/T, then Humility overwrites it — everything, including Humility and the animated enchantments, is 1/1 with no abilities.

rule 613.4b: "Layer 7b: Effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied."
rule 613.7: "An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp."
oracle ed7bdb3e-5c51-4547-9266-76a791e0b2b0#0: "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1."
oracle 59489b46-9d02-4f3c-bcd0-884e7605e9a5#0: "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value."

ruling 59489b46-9d02-4f3c-bcd0-884e7605e9a5/18649cad787b2eba: "But if Humility entered before Opalescence, the following is true: Layer 4: Humility and Worship each become creatures that are still enchantments (Opalescence). Layer 6: Humility and Worship each los…"

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes on both counts, with a twist on the last one.

**Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** is a modal DFC, so you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack (`712.11b`), and only that face is evaluated to see if it can be cast (`712.11c`). Casting the back face means paying Tibalt's {5}{B}{R} — seven mana — from your hand as normal, and you get the emblem and loyalty abilities ("+2: Exile the top card of each player's library.").

In your library, graveyard, hand, or exile it's only Valki: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face" (`712.8a`). So it's a legendary creature card with mana value 2 there, never a planeswalker card.

On the battlefield, whichever face is up is what it is (`712.8f`). So **Vraska's Contempt** can exile it as a creature (Valki side) or as a planeswalker (Tibalt side), and **Kaya's Ghostform** can legally enchant either. But when Ghostform returns the card it comes back front face up: "A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters the battlefield with its front face up by default" (`712.14`). Killing Tibalt and rebuying him with Ghostform gets you a two-mana Valki, not a planeswalker.
citations: oracle 907ae517-22d5-4ac7-bc3a-3f4d5eaeeb57#1: "+2: Exile the top card of each player's library."
rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.11c: "Only the face that will be face up on the stack is evaluated to determine if it can be cast."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
rule 712.14: "A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters the battlefield with its front face up by default."

rows.question: cast Stomp off my bonecrusher giant, it resolved and went to exile. my opp says I can only cast the creature half from exile now, not Stomp again, is that right? also can they counter Stomp with a 'counter target creature spell' effect since the card is a creature?
rows.expected_answer: Your opponent is right. When an Adventure spell resolves it is exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and you may cast the card from exile — but only as the creature (Bonecrusher Giant), not as Stomp again (715.3d). And no, Stomp can't be hit by 'counter target creature spell': while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only its alternative characteristics (715.3a, 715.3b), so it is a red instant, not a creature spell. Everywhere else, including exile, the card is just the creature card Bonecrusher Giant (715.4).

outcome.answer:
Your opponent is right on the first point, wrong on the second.

**Stomp** exiled itself on resolution, and that permission only lets you cast the card as **Bonecrusher Giant** — per `715.3d`, "Instead of putting a spell that was cast as an Adventure into its owner's graveyard as it resolves, its controller exiles it. For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can't be cast as an Adventure this way." (If some *other* effect later lets you cast the card from exile, that effect could let you cast it as an Adventure again.) Timing is normal creature-spell timing: main phase, empty stack.

As for countering: no, a "counter target creature spell" can't touch Stomp. While it's on the stack as an Adventure it's an Instant, not a creature spell — `715.3b`: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics." Color, mana cost, mana value and types all come from the Adventure half only. Once it's cast as Bonecrusher Giant, though, it's a creature spell and is fair game.

rule 715.3b: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."

rows.question: melded my Bruna and Gisela into Brisela and then it got Path to Exiled. does that count as one creature leaving or two for my [[Blood Artist]] type triggers, and do I get one Plains or two off Path?
rows.expected_answer:
Blood Artist does not trigger at all here: Path to Exile exiles Brisela, and Blood Artist
triggers on a creature dying, which means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield
(700.4). Exile is not dying. If Brisela instead died (say, to a Wrath of God), Blood Artist
would trigger exactly once: one permanent left the battlefield, even though the melded
permanent is a single object represented by two cards (712.21, 701.42a). A trigger reading
"whenever a card is put into a graveyard" would see two cards (712.21e). Either way, the
search happens once and Bruna and Gisela both go to exile. It is Brisela's controller who
searches, not the player who cast Path to Exile ("Its controller may search their library
for a basic land card"), and any basic land will do, not only a Plains.

outcome.answer:
Two things: **Blood Artist** doesn't trigger at all here, and you get at most one basic land.

**Path to Exile** exiles the creature; it doesn't put it into a graveyard, so nothing "dies" and **Blood Artist**'s "Whenever this creature or another creature dies" never triggers. If you'd instead had a death or generic leaves‑the‑battlefield trigger, the answer would be once: per `712.21`, when a melded permanent leaves the battlefield "one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone," and `712.21e` says a melded permanent among objects that changed zones "counts as one object that moved" (only effects counting *cards* see two).

So **Brisela, Voice of Nightmares** goes to exile as two cards (you choose their relative timestamp order as they're exiled, per `712.21b`), but it was one creature exiled by one resolution of Path, so its controller "may search their library for a basic land card" exactly once — one Plains, not two.
citations: oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."
oracle d683d985-9888-4d21-8b5f-69e69ce4a03b#0: "Exile target creature. Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle."
rule 712.21: "If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone."
rule 712.21e: "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved."
rule 712.21b: "If a player exiles a melded permanent, that player determines the relative timestamp order of the two cards at that time."

rows.question: old school question. my Waylay (Urza's Saga printing) says 'at end of turn, remove them from the game'. so I cast it during my opponent's end step, the knights survive since the end step already started, and I get to swing with them on my turn right? classic waylay trick
rows.expected_answer: No — that trick was closed by errata. The printed text is not what the card does; you always use the current Oracle wording (108.1), which is 'Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step.' If you cast Waylay in your opponent's end step, the Knights are exiled at that same turn's cleanup step: the game checks for triggered abilities waiting during cleanup, puts the 'beginning of the next cleanup step' trigger on the stack, and then players get priority and another cleanup step follows (514.3a). You never get to attack with them. (Casting it during your opponent's declare-attackers step to get surprise blockers still works.)

outcome.answer:
No — that trick is dead. **Waylay** has been errata'd; its current Oracle text reads "Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step."

Resolving it creates a delayed triggered ability (`603.7`) waiting for the next cleanup step — and that's the very next step of the same turn, since "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup" (`512.1`). When that cleanup step begins, the game checks whether "any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”)"; the trigger goes on the stack, players get priority, it resolves, the Knights are exiled, and then another cleanup step begins (`514.3a`).

So the Knights stick around only for the rest of your opponent's end step — fine as surprise blockers earlier in combat or as sacrifice fodder — but they never reach your turn.

rows.question: my mirage LED says 'play this ability as an interrupt'. so it's a mana ability and I can crack it in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to pay for it right? that way I still have tutor as the last card when I discard
rows.expected_answer: No. Ignore the printed 'interrupt' text and use the current Oracle wording (108.1): 'Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant.' It is still a mana ability — the timing restriction doesn't change that (605.1) — but 'Activate only as an instant' means you may only activate it when you have priority (602.5e), so you can't activate it while paying for a spell the way 605.3a normally allows for mana abilities. The correct play is to cast Infernal Tutor with Tutor as the last card in hand, hold priority, then activate LED in response; when Tutor resolves you are hellbent and the mana is still floating.

outcome.answer:
No. Your Mirage copy's "interrupt" wording is long gone; **Lion's Eye Diamond**'s current Oracle text is "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant." It is still a mana ability — `605.1` says an ability is one "regardless of what other effects they may generate or what timing restrictions (such as “Activate only as an instant”) they may have" — but that restriction means you must follow the timing rules for casting an instant (`602.5e`), i.e. you need priority. You don't have priority in the middle of casting a spell, so you can't crack LED while paying **Infernal Tutor**'s cost. Scryfall's ruling on LED says the same: "it can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant."

And even if you could, it wouldn't do what you want: casting Tutor moves the card to the stack before costs are paid (`601.2a`), so it's not in your hand to be discarded and it isn't the card you reveal.

The real line: pay for Infernal Tutor with other mana, hold priority with Tutor on the stack, then activate LED — your hand empties, Tutor resolves with Hellbent on, and the three mana is waiting for whatever you fetched (it empties at end of step or phase, `106.4`).
citations: oracle ee6099b0-fb1f-42f1-b862-7708c6e36d05#0: "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant."
rule 605.1: "regardless of what other effects they may generate or what timing restrictions (such as “Activate only as an instant”) they may have"
rule 602.5e: "Activated abilities that read “Activate only as an instant” mean the player must follow the timing rules for casting an instant spell, though the ability isn’t actually an instant."

rows.question: ok so I have [[Blood Artist]] out and my opponent wraths with [[Wrath of God]]. Blood Artist dies at the same time as everything else so does it even see the other creatures die? do I drain for all of them or just itself?
rows.expected_answer: Yes, you drain for every creature that died, including Blood Artist itself. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities 'look back in time' (603.10, 603.6c): the game checks the state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield, so it sees every creature that died simultaneously, including itself. All those triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3), and you choose a target player for each one.

outcome.answer:
You drain for every creature that died, including **Blood Artist** itself. So if Wrath kills Blood Artist plus four other creatures, you get five separate triggers.

Blood Artist's ability reads "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life." That's a leaves-the-battlefield trigger, and those look back in time (`603.10a`): the game uses the game state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield with its ability, so it sees all the simultaneous deaths — `603.10`'s own example has an artifact with "Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life" trigger twice even though it's destroyed along with the two creatures. Scryfall confirms: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."

Each trigger goes on the stack separately and you choose a target player for each one, so you can split the life loss among opponents if you like.
citations: oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."
rule 603.10a: "Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities"
rule 603.10: "The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures."
ruling 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d/eaf0e0e76c3621ab: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."
rule 603.3b: "each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn’t another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose"

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

outcome.answer:
Your buddy's got it backwards on one point and right on another. You keep priority after casting, so yes — you can cast a second **Lightning Bolt** before he ever gets to act, and he can't respond until you pass priority: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward" (`117.3c`). He only gets a chance to act once you pass, and nothing resolves until all players pass in succession (`117.4`).

But note the order: the stack is last-in, first-out, so the second Bolt resolves first (`405.2`, `405.5`). If that one kills **Dark Confidant**, the first Bolt's only target is gone when it tries to resolve — it's removed from the stack and does nothing (`608.2b`). And when he does get priority, he can respond to either Bolt with whatever he likes; a spell cast in response resolves before the ones already on the stack (`117.7`).
citations: rule 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward."
rule 117.4: "If all players pass in succession (that is, if all players pass without taking any actions in between passing), the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves"
rule 405.2: "Each time an object is put on the stack, it’s put on top of all objects already there."
rule 405.5: "When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves."

rule 608.2b: "If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve. It’s removed from the stack and, if it’s a spell, put into its owner’s graveyard."
rule 117.7: "the new spell or ability has been cast or activated “in response to” the earlier spell or ability. The new spell or ability will resolve first."
oracle 4457ed35-7c10-48c8-9776-456485fdf070#0: "Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to any target."

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

outcome.answer:
**No, it doesn't die** — and no, you can't respond to the legend rule.

Toughness dips: state-based actions are only checked when a player would get priority, and `704.4` says they "pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability." A spell resolves fully before anyone gets priority (`704.3`), so if the creature's toughness is 0 for an instant mid-resolution but is back above 0 when the spell finishes, `704.5f` never sees a 0-toughness creature and it survives. Scryfall says the same for **Maro**: "If Maro's toughness goes to 0 during the announcement or resolution of a spell or ability and then goes back up above 0 before the end of that announcement or resolution, it won't be put into your graveyard." (Note **Giant Growth** only gives "+3/+3 until end of turn" — it won't save anything from a -X/-X that leaves toughness ≤ 0 when SBAs are actually checked.)

Legend rule: with two **Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer** on the battlefield under your control, `704.5j` applies the moment a player would next get priority — you choose one, the rest go to the graveyard. It's a state-based action, so it "doesn't use the stack" (`704.1`) and nobody gets priority between the second Ragavan arriving and the first being put into the graveyard (`117.5`). There's no window to respond, though you can respond to whatever spell/ability put the second one there, before it resolves.
citations: rule 704.4: "Unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability."

rule 704.3: "Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions s…"
rule 704.5f: "If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard."
rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards."
rule 704.1: "State-based actions don’t use the stack."
rule 117.5: "Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event"

rows.question: I attack with a 5/5 trample that also has deathtouch (Questing Beast) and they block with a 4/4. how much can I trample over? my opponent says I have to assign 4 to the blocker first
rows.expected_answer: The premise is off: Questing Beast is a 4/4 with vigilance, deathtouch and haste, and it does not have trample, so blocked by one creature it assigns all its combat damage to that blocker and nothing goes to the player (510.1c). A good answer says so. For the creature the asker describes, a 5/5 with trample and deathtouch, you only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 and can trample 4 over to the player. Trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blockers before excess goes to the player (702.19b), but any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that purpose (702.2c). Damage assignment for a blocked creature follows 510.1c, then all combat damage is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between (510.2). The 4/4 is then destroyed by deathtouch as an SBA.

outcome.answer:
First, a correction: **Questing Beast** has no trample. Its Oracle text reads "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste" — nothing tramples over. Blocked by the 4/4, it must assign all of its combat damage to that blocker, and none reaches the player (`510.1c`: "If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature").

If you do give it trample from somewhere, your opponent is wrong: you assign only 1 to the blocker and the rest to the player. Trample requires lethal damage on blockers before excess goes through (`702.19b`), and with deathtouch any nonzero combat damage assigned counts as lethal for that check (`702.2c`). So a trampling 5/5 deathtoucher assigns 1 to the 4/4 and 4 to the defending player.
citations: oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"
rule 510.1c: "If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature."

rule 702.19b: "The controller of an attacking creature with trample first assigns damage to the creature(s) blocking it. Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as…"

rule 702.2c: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt."

rows.question: commander q: my commander is [[Kenrith, the Returned King]]. two things: 1) can I run Nicol Bolas, the Ravager since Kenrith's text mentions all 5 colors? and 2) someone bounced Kenrith to my hand with Unsummon - does he go to the command zone or is that only for graveyard/exile?
rows.expected_answer: 1) Yes. Color identity includes mana symbols in the mana cost AND in the rules text (903.4), so Kenrith's identity is WUBRG even though his mana cost is only {4}{W}. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager (UBR) is legal because every color in its identity is in Kenrith's (903.5c). 2) Yes, Kenrith can go to the command zone. If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead - a replacement effect (903.9b). Graveyard/exile use a separate state-based action (903.9a). Either way it's optional.

outcome.answer:
Both yes.

1) **Kenrith, the Returned King**'s color identity is all five colors. Color identity is "the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card's mana cost or rules text" (`903.4`), and Kenrith's rules text contains `{R}`, `{1}{G}`, `{2}{W}`, `{3}{U}` and `{4}{B}` on top of his {4}{W} cost. Since **Nicol Bolas, the Ravager // Nicol Bolas, the Arisen** is blue/black/red on both faces (the back face counts too, per `903.4d`), every color in its identity is in Kenrith's, so it's legal per `903.5c`. With a WUBRG commander you can run any card that's otherwise legal.

2) He can go to the command zone. `903.9a` (graveyard/exile) is the state-based-action version, but `903.9b` covers hand and library: "If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead." That's a replacement effect, so you choose as **Unsummon** resolves — if you let him land in your hand, he stays there.

oracle d209b948-9afb-4fd1-a961-72c87282878c#0: "{4}{B}: Put target creature card from a graveyard onto the battlefield under its owner's control."
rule 903.4: "The color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text"
rule 903.4d: "The back face of a double-faced card (see rule 712) is included when determining a card’s color identity."

rows.question: commander damage question. I've been hit for 15 by my opponent's Rafiq. she then copies it with a Clone and hits me for 6 more with the clone. do I lose? also does the 21 count noncombat damage like from Fling?
rows.expected_answer: No to both. A player loses when they've been dealt 21 or more COMBAT damage by the SAME commander over the course of the game (903.10a; checked as a state-based action, 704.6c). The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 damage isn't commander damage - you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq. Fling damage is noncombat, so it never counts toward the 21 either; it just reduces your life total normally.

outcome.answer:
No, you don't lose, and no, Fling damage doesn't count.

The Clone isn't a commander. It's a permanent copying a commander, and 903.3 is explicit: "A permanent that's copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player's graveyard) is not a commander." Being a copy of **Rafiq of the Many** copies its copiable characteristics, not the commander designation, which per 903.3 "is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself." So the Clone's 6 damage is just ordinary combat damage — your commander-damage tally from Rafiq stays at 15 (you'd need 6 more from the real Rafiq).

As for **Fling**: the state-based action only counts combat damage — "A player who's been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game" (903.10a). Fling's damage is dealt by Fling anyway, not by the commander, and it isn't combat damage, so it never adds to the 21. It still takes your life total down normally, of course.
citations: rule 903.3: "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander."
rule 903.3: "This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself."
rule 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."
oracle 24227761-b50e-4b9e-93a2-e82d053b3e3d#0: "Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature's power to any target."

rows.question: two quick ones. 1) if I tap all my lands during my upkeep does that mana stick around so I can cast the mind sculptor in my main phase? 2) when I'm casting snappy can I tap lands in the middle of casting it or do I have to float the mana first?
rows.expected_answer: 1) No. Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana added during your upkeep is lost before your main phase (106.4). Tap the lands in your main phase instead. 2) Yes. Casting a spell includes a step where, if the total cost includes mana, you get a chance to activate mana abilities such as tapping lands (601.2g), and only then do you pay the total cost (601.2h). You do not need to float mana before announcing the spell.

outcome.answer:
**1) No.** Mana doesn't survive the step it was made in — "Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana" (`106.4`). Mana floated in your upkeep is gone at the end of the upkeep step, long before your precombat main phase; you'd lose it again at the end of the draw step too. Tap your lands in the main phase when you actually cast **Jace, the Mind Sculptor**.

**2) You can tap mid-cast.** After the total cost is locked in, "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities" — and mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid (`601.2g`). A player may activate a mana ability "whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment... even if it's in the middle of casting or resolving a spell" (`605.3a`). So you announce **Snapcaster Mage**, lock in the cost, then tap lands for exactly what you need. Floating first is legal but unnecessary — and riskier, since leftover mana is wasted at end of step.
citations: rule 106.4: "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana."

rule 601.2g: "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."

rule 605.3a: "A player may activate an activated mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks …"

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.
